Prior Authorization Services

Approval Secured Before the Procedure, Not Chased After It

Prior authorization is a payer's requirement that certain procedures, imaging, medications or admissions be approved in advance before the payer agrees to cover them. It's a utilization management tool insurers use to confirm a service is medically necessary, that it's actually covered under the patient's plan, and that a lower-cost alternative wasn't overlooked, before money changes hands.

Hundreds of distinct services can require it, and the rules differ by payer, by plan, and often by state. That variability is exactly what makes tracking every requirement manually one of the most error-prone parts of scheduling care. A service that needed authorization last year under one plan might not need it this year, or might need it from a different department entirely.

Miss an authorization requirement and the consequences land on both sides at once. The practice risks a denied claim for a service already delivered, with little recourse beyond an appeal. The patient risks a delayed procedure, a canceled appointment, or an unexpected bill for something they assumed was covered.

PMEX identifies authorization requirements at scheduling, gathers the exact documentation a payer will ask for, submits the request in the payer's required format, and tracks it to a decision, so a procedure is never delayed by paperwork that could have been handled days earlier.

What Typically Requires Authorization

Coverage Varies by Payer, but These Categories Come Up Constantly

Advanced Imaging

MRI, CT and PET scans almost always require pre-approval before scheduling.

Elective Surgical Procedures

Non-emergency surgeries typically need documented medical necessity approval.

Specialty & Brand Medications

High-cost drugs are frequently gated behind step-therapy and authorization rules.

Durable Medical Equipment

Wheelchairs, CPAP machines and similar equipment usually need prior approval.

Physical & Occupational Therapy

Ongoing therapy plans often require authorization renewal after a set number of visits.

Inpatient Admissions

Non-emergency admissions typically require notification and approval in advance.

Behavioral Health Services

Certain levels of behavioral health care require authorization before treatment starts.

Out-of-Network Referrals

Referrals outside a plan's network almost always require prior approval.

Urgent & Expedited Requests

When a Standard Timeline Isn't an Option

Most payers offer an expedited review path for cases where a delay could seriously jeopardize a patient's health. PMEX identifies when a request qualifies for expedited handling and files it accordingly, so urgent care is never held up by a routine authorization timeline.

If an authorization is denied and the situation calls for it, PMEX coordinates a peer-to-peer review, connecting the treating provider directly with the payer's medical reviewer to make the clinical case in real time.

Standard Requests

Routine services processed within the payer's normal review window, typically a few business days.

Expedited Requests

Time-sensitive cases flagged and routed for faster payer review, often within 24 to 72 hours.

Peer-to-Peer Review

Contested authorizations escalated to a direct clinical conversation between provider and payer reviewer.

Prior Authorization: Frequently Asked Questions

Payers use prior authorization to confirm a service is medically necessary and covered under the patient's plan before agreeing to pay for it, and to steer utilization toward cost-effective options where appropriate.

Standard requests often take a few business days, while expedited review is available for urgent cases and can move much faster. PMEX submits early enough that most requests clear well before the scheduled date.

A denied authorization is followed up with additional clinical documentation, a formal appeal, or a peer-to-peer review for contested cases, using the same escalation process PMEX applies to claim denials.

It's a direct conversation between the treating provider and the payer's medical reviewer, used when a standard authorization request is denied and the clinical case needs to be made in real time rather than in writing.

Yes, most authorizations carry an expiration window. PMEX tracks approval dates against the scheduled visit and flags anything at risk of expiring before it happens.

Yes. Authorization requests are handled for procedures, imaging, durable medical equipment and specialty or brand-name medications, following each payer's specific submission process for each category.
